title: Building and delivering a winning speech
objective: Structure, rehearse and deliver a prepared or extemporaneous speech that holds an audience and fits the time limit.
body:
Speaking events such as Prepared Presentation and Extemporaneous Speech are scored on two things at once: what you say and how you say it. Judges reward a clear message, logical organization, confident delivery and staying within the time limit. A brilliant idea delivered in a rambling way usually loses to a simpler idea delivered with focus.

**Start with one core message.** Before outlining, write a single sentence that states your point, your *thesis*. Every story, statistic and slide should support it. If a detail does not, cut it.

**Use a simple structure.**
1. *Introduction:* an attention-getter (a question, short story or striking fact), the thesis and a preview of your main points.
2. *Body:* two or three main points, each with support such as an example, data or an expert view, linked by clear *transitions* ('That cost leads to a second problem...').
3. *Conclusion:* a summary of the points and a memorable closing line that echoes the opening.

**Adapt to the format.** In a prepared speech you can polish wording and rehearse with visual aids, but speak from brief notes rather than reading a script. In extemporaneous speaking you get a topic and a short prep period, so use a repeatable plan: choose your thesis in the first minute, jot three points with one example each, write your first and last sentences, then rehearse the opening silently. If you are teaching a lesson, as in Future Technology and Engineering Teacher, state a measurable objective ('students will be able to...') and check for understanding before you finish.

**Deliver with purpose.**
- *Eye contact:* sweep the whole room and hold each look for a sentence or so.
- *Voice:* vary pace, volume and pitch; pause before and after key ideas.
- *Body:* stand balanced, use natural gestures and avoid pacing or fidgeting.
- *Filler words:* replace 'um' and 'like' with a short silent pause.

**Visual aids support the speaker; they do not replace you.** Use few words per slide, large readable type and one idea per slide. If the audience is reading, they are not listening.

**Practice against the clock.** Rehearse aloud, time yourself and decide in advance what you would cut if you run long. Going over the limit usually costs points.

A common mistake is memorizing a script word for word. When you lose your place, you freeze. Memorize your structure, your opening and your closing, and speak the middle from key words.
examples: An extemporaneous competitor draws the topic 'Should schools limit phone use in class?' She spends the first minute choosing a thesis (limit phones during instruction, allow them at lunch), then writes three points, distraction, safety and teaching digital responsibility, each with one example.

A Prepared Presentation speaker rehearses a talk with a 5-minute limit and finishes in 5:40. He cuts the weakest of three supporting stories and one slide of statistics, bringing the talk to 4:35 and leaving room for pauses.
A presenter replaces a slide containing 90 words with one photo and a six-word headline, and moves the details into what she says aloud.

questions.stem: A speaker's outline has an attention-getter, three main points and a closing line, but after the speech the audience could not say what it was about. What is most likely missing?
choices: A clear thesis that every main point supports
More statistics inside each main point
A longer story in the introduction
Extra slides with detailed text
questions.explanation: The thesis is the one-sentence message that ties the points together. Without it, even well-supported points feel unconnected, and adding more detail does not fix that.

questions.stem: You draw an extemporaneous speaking topic and have a short preparation period. What is the best first step?
choices: Write out the entire speech word for word
Decide on a one-sentence thesis that answers the topic
Sketch visuals to hold up during the speech
Memorize as many statistics on the subject as possible
questions.explanation: Choosing a thesis first gives every later decision a direction. Writing a full script wastes limited prep time and encourages reading instead of speaking.

questions.stem: Which sentence works best as a transition between two main points?
choices: Thank you all for listening to my presentation today.
My name is Jordan, and I will be speaking about energy.
Beyond the cost to families, the new policy also affects local businesses.
According to a recent survey, most students walk to school.
questions.explanation: A transition links the point just finished (cost to families) to the next one (local businesses). The other sentences are a closing, an introduction and a piece of evidence.

questions.stem: During rehearsal, a speaker says 'um' between almost every sentence. What is the most effective fix?
choices: Speak faster so there is no room for fillers
Read the speech directly from a full script
Add more slides to glance at between sentences
Replace each filler with a brief silent pause
questions.explanation: A short pause sounds confident and gives the speaker time to think, which is what the filler was doing. Speeding up usually creates more fillers, not fewer.

questions.stem: A speech must run 3 to 5 minutes. In rehearsal it runs 5 minutes 45 seconds. Which change best fixes the problem while protecting the message?
choices: Cut the weakest supporting example and its slide
Talk faster through the entire speech
Skip the conclusion to save time
Remove the thesis from the introduction
questions.explanation: Cutting the least important support shortens the speech while keeping the thesis, structure and conclusion intact. Rushing hurts clarity, and dropping the conclusion or thesis weakens the message.

questions.stem: Which slide design best supports a speaker during a presentation?
choices: Full paragraphs so the audience can read along
One idea per slide with a short headline and a large image
Several charts on each slide to show all the data at once
Small text so more detail fits on every slide
questions.explanation: Simple slides keep attention on the speaker and make one point at a time easy to see. Dense text and crowded charts compete with the speaker for attention.

questions.stem: A competitor plans to memorize her 5-minute speech word for word. What is the main risk of this approach?
choices: Judges award no points for memorized content
A memorized speech always runs too short
Losing one word can make her freeze and break her flow
Memorizing prevents her from using any visual aids
questions.explanation: Word-for-word memorization depends on recalling an exact sequence, so a single slip can derail the speech. Memorizing the structure, opening and closing is more resilient.

questions.stem: A Future Technology and Engineering Teacher competitor is planning a short lesson. Which lesson objective is written most effectively?
choices: Students will understand gears.
Students will appreciate the importance of engineering.
Students will learn a lot about simple machines.
Students will be able to calculate the gear ratio of a two-gear system.
questions.explanation: A strong objective names an observable, measurable action (calculate a gear ratio), so the teacher can check whether students met it. 'Understand' and 'appreciate' cannot be directly observed.

flashcards.definition: The single sentence that states the main point of a speech, which every part of the speech supports.
An opening question, short story or striking fact that draws the audience in before the thesis.
A phrase or sentence that links one main point to the next so the audience can follow the structure.
A speech delivered from brief notes after a short preparation period on an assigned topic.
A lesson goal stated as an observable action, such as 'students will be able to calculate,' that can be checked.
